event: Evercore ISI 3rd Annual Consumer and Retail Conference
rows: Evercore ISI 3rd Annual Consumer and Retail Conference
Food Service Share of Pepsi Sales
Management positioned Celsius as the leader of the 'second wave' of energy drinks, evolved from a niche fitness brand into a strong #3 with an ~8% national share.
Differentiation rests on three megatrends: better-for-you without sacrificing flavor, more function (a clinically studied thermogenic), and a premium fitness-lifestyle positioning.
The community Celsius built around the brand as a daily fitness lifestyle is the core differentiator vs the crowded new-wave field (C4, Ghost, ZOA, A-Shock, Alani Nu).
High incrementality - 68% of consumption incremental (24% new-to-category, 44% user intensification) - resonates with retailers as not just brand shifting.
Celsius over-indexes with Hispanic and African-American consumers; the demo is now ~50/50 male/female, shifting incrementally toward males as convenience accelerates.
Food service reached ~10% of Pepsi revenue after only ~3 months - a 'huge unlock' showing Celsius is broader than energy; basket-ring/delivery data still being captured.
Management shifted its tone from 'going after energy' to a 'total beverage play.'
The competitive 'street war' is intensifying - Red Bull responded to share loss with strong January/February promotional activity (mainly grocery, also convenience) that has since normalized.
Pepsi enables national execution and consistency that the prior fragmented network of 300+ independent distributors could not - Celsius could not compete at this level without Pepsi.
Amazon strength (~19% share, #2) shows no cannibalization despite distribution expansion (DSD, club ~$50M Q1) and 140% scan growth - 'all tides are rising.'
The Amazon channel margin question was explicitly asked by the moderator but never answered by management.
Core-portfolio focus comes first (timing, sequencing, discipline); adjacent categories and Pepsi-portfolio white space are being evaluated but not yet a priority.
A lower-caffeine product is confirmed 'down the road for sure' as a potential meal-occasion expansion, but no timing or specification given; Celsius also has a 16-ounce line.
The category is growing 10-15% with retailers allocating more shelf space to energy; ~13.6 items per store leaves runway for SKU and pack-size innovation, with new flavors in the 2024 pipeline.
Health/fitness as a lifestyle is a structural global tailwind, intensified post-pandemic; energy is mainstreaming as CSD consumers explore the category.
For less-familiar investors, what distinguishes Celsius from the rest of the 'second wave' of new-wave energy brands (C4, Ghost, ZOA, A-Shock, Alani Nu) in branding, product and liquid?

John Fieldly recounted the brand's evolution - historically blocked from traditional convenience, built through fitness, grocery, mass drug and club, with convenience now the 'last frontier.' Toby David noted Celsius is a strong #3 building a delta vs #4/#5 while closing on Red Bull and Monster. Fieldly said the differentiation is the community built as a daily fitness lifestyle, hitting three megatrends: better-for-you without sacrificing flavor, more function (a clinically studied thermogenic), and a premium fitness-lifestyle positioning.
Mainstreaming the category & big-player energy launches
What are the learnings on why the big players' energy launches (Coke Energy, Mountain Dew Energy) stumbled, and how does Celsius play into mainstreaming the category?

John Fieldly: bringing CSD consumers into energy is positive and differentiating - Celsius is 'more inviting,' with great core flavors (a new lemon lime as a Walmart lead launch) and fun Vibe flavors, non-aggressive packaging and a high take rate building loyalty; he cited the food-service unlock (~10% of Q1 Pepsi sales) as evidence Celsius is broader than energy, with opportunity in lunch occasions and Grubhub delivery basket rings.
What is Celsius's gender, income and demographic mix, and has it stayed constant or is growth coming from new demographics?

John Fieldly: historically the brand skewed older (25-40 target), ~50-50 male/female (slightly female), higher income given fitness/vitamin/Amazon channels. Toby David: today still close to 50-50 but shifting incrementally toward males as convenience accelerates, over-indexing with Hispanic and African-American consumers; reiterated 24% new-to-category, 44% user intensification, 68% incremental - 'not just brand shifting.'
Does the Hispanic/African-American over-indexing reflect specific targeting, the company's strong states (California, Florida), or different targeting by other energy drinks?

Toby David: the welcoming, clean, fruit-forward, lower-sugar packaging appeals broadly; there may be a geographic effect given strength in Southern California, Dallas and South Florida, and an ethno-marketing opportunity Celsius has never pursued. John Fieldly: the three megatrends are universal and global, gaining strength post-pandemic, and the non-aggressive, no-crash/no-jitters product drives broad appeal.
Red Bull and Monster took pricing in fall 2022 but promo is increasing, and Red Bull - losing share - is starting to hit the promo button; how should we think about that dynamic?

John Fieldly: there is more promo this summer than last; the category historically runs 24-28 promotional weeks, so Celsius will run deals (retailers ask for them), and there is 'plenty of pricing for all of us' with the category growing 10-15%. Toby David: Red Bull took strong January/February promotional activity (mainly grocery, also convenience) that has since normalized; it is a 'street war' and a fight for space - Celsius is well situated to defend, with Pepsi enabling national field execution vs the prior fragmented ~300-distributor network.
Does being aligned with Pepsi give Celsius an advantage, and will the big players think twice about how they compete tactically against a Pepsi-aligned Celsius?

John Fieldly: competition is constant, but Pepsi's key advantage is enabling national execution and consistency - the prior fragmented network of 300+ independent distributors could not execute national programs with national retailers (7-Eleven, CVS), limiting Celsius to regional execution; he also praised Big Geyser's strong execution in New York.
The two big competitors have very different strategies - where is Celsius's strategy developing over the next three-to-five years, and could food occasions lead to a different liquid?

John Fieldly: Celsius is refining a three-to-five-year strategy with opportunities in adjacent categories - including white space within the Pepsi portfolio - but the immediate focus is the core portfolio, which has a long runway requiring timing, sequencing and discipline; growth levers include additional placements (~13.6 items per store), pack-size innovation, variety/large packs, new 2024 flavors, and the powder business.
Is the Amazon channel the same or a different consumer, are the margins incremental or dilutive, and is a strong Amazon presence a positive or a challenge with retailers?

Toby David: Celsius holds a ~19% Amazon share (6-7 points ahead of Red Bull, just behind Monster), built since 2020 even as DSD and club (~$50M Q1 Costco, ~$200M run rate) expanded - with 140% scan growth and no cannibalization; the Amazon consumer is 'everybody.' John Fieldly: Celsius always embraced omnichannel; it has been 'contentious' with some retailers as Amazon scaled but those challenges were worked through. The direct question on Amazon margins was not answered.
Amazon growth rate vs scan data
Is the growth rate on Amazon faster or slower than what is seen in scanner data?
Toby David: Amazon growth has been very strong but maybe not quite as strong as the triple-digit numbers seen in scan data.
Given the stock's run and an ~8-9% share, some would call it a day - what is the pitch to investors for the future?

John Fieldly recapped the journey - the convenience/OTS unlock driving the move to DSD then Pepsi, enabling national strategic execution - and the food-service unlock showing consumption beyond traditional energy; management shifted tone from 'going after energy' to a 'total beverage play,' citing Gen Z's lower fountain-drink use and the rise of delivery; the ~22% South Florida share shows market-level potential well above the 8% national level across 23+ key markets.
Celsius is 200mg caffeine - is a lower-caffeine product to hit meal/other occasions on the radar, given competitors at 150mg, 120mg and hybrid drinks at 80mg?

John Fieldly: there are opportunities in different pack sizes (Celsius has a 16-ounce line) and there could be a lighter-caffeinated product down the line, confirming a lower-caffeinated opportunity 'down the road for sure,' though he declined to share specifics from the plans.
